content: The approach of extrapolating drug-drug interaction data from adults to children has been supported by direct pharmacokinetic data in children. This data justifies the use of dolutegravir (DTG) administered twice daily for children weighing more than 25 kg. The Paediatric Antiretroviral Working Group emphasizes the importance of continuing to collect confirmatory evidence for children in lower weight bands. However, they endorse the immediate adoption of twice-daily DTG dosing in combination with rifampicin for all children at least four weeks old and weighing at least 3 kg. The heat-stable tablet formulation of lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. For children weighing 14–<25 kg, one 200/50 mg tablet can be given in the morning and one in the evening. For children weighing 25–<35 kg, two tablets can be given in the morning and one in the evening. The liquid formulation of LPV/r requires a cold chain for transport and storage, while the pellet formulation is not recommended for infants younger than three months. Additional details on administering LPV/r pellets are available. The dosing schedule provided also applies to equivalent solid dosage forms, such as LPV/r granules, which have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use starting at two weeks of age. For super-boosting with ritonavir (RTV) to achieve a 1:1 ratio with LPV in milligrams, a study has supported this approach for young children receiving LPV/r. RTV oral solution dosing is based on trial-tested regimens, with 5 mg once daily for neonates weighing 2–<4 kg, 25 mg once daily for infants weighing 4–<8 kg, and 50 mg once daily for children weighing more than 8 kg. LPV/r is administered twice daily after the first week of life, with 40/10 mg once daily for neonates weighing 2–<4 kg and 80/20 mg once daily for infants weighing more than 4 kg. This simplified dosing was developed using a WHO generic tool based on established nevirapine prophylactic targets. In recent years, improved antiretroviral (ARV) drug formulations for children, such as dispersible and scored fixed-dose combination tablets, have replaced traditional liquid formulations. These products have simplified HIV treatment delivery for children in low-income settings. However, the proliferation of options has led to a fragmentation of demand across multiple formulations, creating supply chain instability and complicating procurement. The ARV Procurement Working Group and the Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations Network provide formulary guidance to programs for selecting optimal ARV drugs for children, based on robust criteria. The Optimal Formulary, first developed in 2011 and revised in December 2020, now includes seven products that deliver recommended firstand second-line regimens across all weight bands for children. Programs are encouraged to procure dosage forms included in the Optimal ARV Formulary for Children. During transitional periods or special circumstances (e.g., neonatal treatment, TB co-treatment, or third-line ART), dosage forms from the ARV Limited-use Formulary are sufficient to provide appropriate dosing across weight bands. The urgent need for better age-appropriate formulations for infants and children living with HIV remains a priority. An additional solid fixed-dose combination formulation (ABC/3TC/LPV/r granules) is in the final stages of approval. The availability of co-formulated darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) in a heat-stable fixed-dose combination is critical for facilitating treatment sequencing and uptake of future secondand third-line regimens for children. Furthermore, the central role of dolutegravir (DTG) and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) in optimizing dosing, sequencing, and harmonization across age groups has been highlighted. WHO will continue to work towards simplifying prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance while collaborating with the pharmaceutical industry and other partners to develop practical recommendations for formulations that can safely accelerate the scaling up of ART for children.
